evidence_quotes.quote: The in force national and county water policies, strategies, and plans for the case study areas were critically reviewed. The status of aquifer knowledge, water access disparities, competing uses, and risks was evaluated from critical literature reviews and data compilation, fieldwork, and analysis of indicator datasets from the Kenya 2009 census.

Five towns in Kenya in which the author has had substantial field experience have been selected as a multitown cohort of case studies for this report: Kisumu City and the town of Nakuru are in the sub-humid zones; Lodwar and Wajir towns are in the arid zones; and, the town of Msambweni is in the semi-arid zone.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 11, Findings - Water access disparities
evidence_quotes.quote: As of 2010, the existing water supply system could provide only 36 L/day (L/d) of water on average in Kenya, though it is required to provide 60 L/day even for populations in low class housing, according to the national standard (Table 5).

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 13, Findings - Challenges and gaps
evidence_quotes.quote: None of them mention NWMP 2030, and only the Nakuru CIDP alludes to the development of a county water master plan.

The 2016 Act has also taken cognisance of public participation in the formulation and periodic revision of the strategies, and private sector participation in water development and services provision.

country.comment: All five urban case-study towns (Kisumu City, Nakuru, Lodwar, Wajir, and Msambweni) and the national/county legal and policy frameworks examined are in Kenya.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title and Abstract; PDF p. 2, Materials and methods

effect_estimate.comment: No inferential statistical model or causal effect estimate is reported; empirical results consist of descriptive census/regulatory water-access and service metrics across the 5 towns paired with a doctrinal and planning audit of national water laws/strategies and 5 County Integrated Development Plans (CIDPs).
effect_estimate.value: Descriptive and policy-audit synthesis (no regression effect estimate reported): Across urban Kenya (N = 11.844 million, 2009 Census), 34.9% used piped water and 14.7% had water piped into dwellings, while combined piped access (piped + piped into dwelling) varied across the 5 case-study towns from 78.3% in Nakuru (56.3% + 22.0%), 51.8% in Lodwar (41.2% + 10.6%), and 35.5% in Kisumu (30.0% + 5.5%) to 2.0% in Msambweni (1.6% + 0.4%) and 1.6% in Wajir (1.3% + 0.3%), where residents relied predominantly on shallow wells (Wajir: 39.4% protected, 55.9% unprotected) and boreholes/shallow wells (Msambweni: 41.2% borehole, 18.6% protected well, 27.8% unprotected well). Average supply in Kenya was 36 L/day in 2010 vs the 60 L/day national minimum standard (22.5 L/day in Kisumu informal settlements; 2014/2015 served-population supply of 47 L/day in Kisumu, 34 L/day in Nakuru, and 10 L/day in Lodwar, with non-revenue water at 49%, 37%, and 40%, respectively, vs WASREB's 20% target). Policy/institutional audit found that only 1 of 10 NWRMS 2007 groundwater tasks was fully achieved by 2018 (6 partially, 3 not achieved), NWMP 2030 targets only ~5% of urban water demand from groundwater despite arid/sub-humid towns relying heavily on aquifers, and none of the 5 audited CIDPs (2013–2017) referenced NWMP 2030, reflecting weak national-county coordination and low county technical/institutional capacity.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 10–14, Sections 'Water access disparities' and 'Governance and management framework'; Table 3 (PDF p. 11); Table 4 (PDF p. 12); Table 5 (PDF p. 14)

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at <= 2 by design ceiling (Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework). Assigned 1 because the study empirically documents planning, regulatory, and national-county coordination gaps in statutes, strategies, and CIDPs alongside descriptive 2009 census and utility water-access disparities across towns and planned/informal settlements, but does not directly observe the administrative/legal mechanisms operating on household water access (census data from 2009 predate the 2010 devolution, 2013–2017 CIDPs, and Water Act 2016) or test causal effects.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines national and county water/development planning and planned vs unplanned settlement infrastructure reach (planning), horizontal fragmentation across NWMP 2030, NWRMS, NWSS, and water agencies (institutional_fragmentation), vertical national-county devolution alignment between national strategies and County Integrated Development Plans (political_coordination), public and private sector participation under the Water Act 2016 and decentralised co-management (participation), and regulatory monitoring/permitting/standards oversight under WRA and WASREB (ENFORCEMENT).
